The speed in which bulk bins are turned over depends heavily on the popularity of the contents. I have several stores I frequent based on their weekly sales, but the one store in my area that gathers my near sole attention to their bulk bins is Winco Foods, an employee-owned chain heavily centered through Washington, Oregon, California, with stores infiltrating through Nevada, Utah, Idaho and, big jump, into the center of Texas.

![](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-17d77bff389f7ee735319a53a22f7c2a.webp)

The bulk bin corner of each store is huge in comparison to what I’ve seen in other stores and virtually everything you see may be ordered in a 20 pound bag online, for a deeper discount than even the bin price, and picked up in the store.

Every time I’m shopping at my local store, there is a restock clerk in this area tidying or refilling or pulling the scanty remains of a large bottom bin to drop in a new fresh bag. The turnover here is heavy but the prices are truly sweet, making the avid interest reasonable. What pleases me is that some of these bins contain name brands, such as Bob’s Red Mill ground grains or even Lundberg rice. Effort is obvious to offer the customer the best available to their buyers.

About the only bins I don’t see refilled often is the large paper-wrapped candy in barrels, but then these candies are not at a storage or contamination risk. Personally I seldom buy the sweet ingredients or loose, unwrapped candies as those are fairly hard to keep wandering bare fingers away. You know it happens, the clerks know as well.

I have shopped bulk bins in other stores but find there is proof of my own witness that some stores do keep after bulk bins and much of that focus depends on individual management. If the lingering idea of grubby fingers in a bin is too repellent, don’t dig into the open barrels. Use the chute-dispensing units above as the contents for these can only be man-handled by gloved staff.

During my time working in both management and part time capacities at a large supermarket, I can tell you that the evolution of what happens with food past its sell by date has been pretty fascinating. There is a distinction to note that there are generally several dates associated with food. There is a sell by date, a best by date and an expiration date.

The short answer to your question is, yes, a lot of food gets thrown out.

The long answer is that most supermarkets do a very good job of minimizing this waste. Almost all departments, especially ones with perishable items, order to sell out and should come very close to running out before their next order arrives. Think about that the next time your supermarket is out of fresh wild salmon. Would they really bring in one extra twenty pound case just to sell you an eight ounce fillet at 8PM the night before fresh fish arrives? Depends on the market and how aggressively the store wants to capture sales, but mostly, no.

The blanket rule for food past its expiration date is this, if it is unsafe in any way, shape or form, it gets thrown out. They find a way to use almost everything else.

Produce \- Fruits and vegetables don't come with clear expiration dates. I will tell you that you will probably never see a banana that's turning brown on the racks in the produce department. If some produce isn't sell-able it usually gets shopped around the store. A department that handles any type of prepared foods will use these items to make items for hot bars, salad bars, soups, etc. The same goes for meat and seafood that is past its sell by date but still within its best by date.

Composting seems like the natural answer for all the other produce that can't be used. This issue has been explored and explored at our supermarket and there are two major roadblocks to seeing it in action.

1. Storage \- Most farms are generally farther away from urbanized (or suburbanized) stores. Because produce deteriorates rather quickly farms would have to pick up compostable produce on a daily basis. Storage at the market is not an option because a large, rotting pile of fruit would attract all sorts of unwanted pests to the store. Daily pickup is difficult and would the extra monetary and green cost of the freight and labor make up for the produce that would be picked up? The logistics of the operation are more involved than one might initially think.
2. Recalls \- Unfortunately, recalls due to contaminated fruits and vegetables do happen. Many of them happen after the produce has been in the store for some time. If the store composts melons, and those same melons are recalled two days later due to a possible salmonella contamination, then you have potentially deadly compost making its way around your local farms. I am neither an expert in food-borne illness nor composting, so I don't know if there is any validity to this concern, but I do know it sounds scary. And that's enough to put the issue on the back burner.

Bakery \- Almost all old baked goods get donated to the local food bank which disperses it to not for profit agencies in the area. Every morning a big shopping cart of old muffins, donuts and bread makes it way to the back dock and every morning at 10AM a van rolls around and picks it up.

Meat and Seafood \- Lately, within the past couple of months, they've been testing out freezing meats that have just passed sell by date and donating these to the local soup kitchens. Again, this is still in its infancy and some issues have arisen that have taken the logistics of this back to the drawing board. The main issue becomes, and always comes back too, safety. Just because a product makes it to its final consumer in a frozen state doesn't mean its 100% safe. What happened to the product in the mean time? Traceability is of paramount importance until it gets to the store, but the cost involved with continuing that traceability until it reaches donations is economically unfeasible.

Grocery and Dairy \- Unfortunately, for the same reasons Meat and Seafood can't be donated, many refrigerated, expired dairy products don't make the list. The good news is that very few items get thrown out. Longer shelf lives, higher demand and tight orders ensures that they only dairy products that really get thrown out are the damaged ones that aren't safe for consumption anyways.

Grocery items are given to food banks. I'm sure some smaller markets donate directly. At our store, everything expired is packed and freighted to headquarters and they distribute the goods evenly among the communities that our supermarket are located in. The extra freight may seem wasteful but I am assuming they record their donations for tax deduction purposes.

I've had the good fortune to spend some time volunteering at food banks. They have different expiration dates for products which I assume are regulated by some sort of government agency. For example, (I'm just using an arbitrary example, I don't remember the exact dates and figures) canned beans may be ok for two years past the date on the can whereas boxed pasta is good for six months past the date on the box. The majority of my volunteer time at the food banks was spent sorting through the mountains of canned goods and checking expiration dates to see what was still deemed safe and what wasn't.

So basically, if it's safe it gets donated. If it's not, it gets thrown out. Definitely some food for thought.

I can think of a couple of reasons. First, it would be prohibitively expensive to sort through the produce and eliminate the pieces with too much cosmetic damage to appeal to consumers. Second, in many cases the skin of overripe produce has been broken. This is unsanitary, as it allows filth and bacteria to come in contact with the parts we eat.

Occasionally, Mother Nature delivers a huge crop that the markets just can't absorb. In this case, producers and processors try to work with local food banks or "gleaners" to minimize waste, but these schemes are hard to carry out. There is a small time window, and most people do not like to pick produce after more than half an hour or so.

Every year, British supermarkets process millions of tonnes of fresh food. Yet an unsold steak rarely reaches a landfill—instead, it is discounted, donated, or digested into electricity.

The frontline defense against food waste is the “yellow sticker” culture. Supermarkets like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, and Asda employ a dynamic discounting system for products approaching their expiration date. Staff continuously monitor fresh produce, meat, and dairy aisles, applying progressive markdowns—often ending in a final wave of heavy discounts just before the store closes.

![](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-6f8c7e3995b32c368f404b281c54358f)

Discounted bread with 'reduced to clear' yellow stickers in a Sainsbury's supermarket. Photo by [Philafrenzy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yellow_sticker_bread_reduced_to_clear_in_Sainsbury%27s_supermarket.jpg) is licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0).

In recent years, retailers have also aggressively targeted premature waste at the source by removing "Best Before" dates from hundreds of lines of fresh fruit and vegetables. Stores like Waitrose, Marks & Spencer, and Asda now rely on staff visual checks rather than arbitrary dates to pull spoiled items, which extends the shelf life of perfectly edible food both in-store and in consumers' homes.

When food cannot be sold, redistribution networks step in. Surplus stock is routinely channeled to charities through integrated logistics partnerships with organizations like FareShare and the Trussell Trust. These charities collect edible, unsold food from supermarket distribution centers and deliver it to community kitchens and food banks. Direct-to-consumer apps have also become deeply embedded in the UK retail ecosystem. Platforms like Too Good To Go allow customers to purchase “magic bags” of unsold, mixed grocery items at a fraction of their retail price at the end of the day, effectively crowd-sourcing the redistribution process.

Finally, food that is no longer fit for human consumption is diverted from the landfill. Bakery waste is frequently processed into animal feed. The remaining organic waste—such as spoiled vegetables or damaged meat—is sent to anaerobic digestion plants. These industrial facilities use microorganisms to break down the food waste in the absence of oxygen, capturing the resulting biogas to generate electricity or heat, and producing a nutrient-rich digestate that farmers use as fertilizer.

# 50 Ways to Save Money Shopping in Bulk
## Shop At A Busy Store
Busy stores have the most turnover, which means bulk-bin items are more likely to be fresh.

## Check For Freshness
![woman holding her nose because of a bad smell](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_94wPrM8.jpg)PhotoMediaGroup/shutterstock

Most bulk bins have a strict no-sampling policy, so shoppers must rely on smell and sight to check for signs of spoilage. If you get a whiff of something funky, or see discoloration, it’s best to move on.

## Try New Things
They say variety is the spice of life, and bulk bins are full of new smells, textures, and flavors to try.

## Rotate Goods
Keeping things fresh and exciting is key to working through a large stash of bulk items.

# 50 Ways to Save Money Shopping in Bulk

Published February 21, 2017•Updated October 28, 2025

•


By

[Tess Rose Lampert](https://www.cheapism.com/tess-rose-lampert/ "Posts by Tess Rose Lampert")

Like what we have to say? [Add cheapism.com as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cheapism.com)

![bulk nuts and fruit in grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original-570x379.jpg)Blue Lemon Photo/shutterstock

Buying from bulk bins is an easy way to save at the supermarket. These days bulk bins contain an ever wider array of goods, from classic granolas, dry beans, and grains to exotic dried fruits, cooking oils, and even sundries such as body lotion and shampoo. Follow these tips to maximize bulk-bin savings.

## Do The Math

![woman in her kitchen writing a grocery list with laptop, calculator, pen, and pencil](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_8wKdTtc.jpg)Tepikina Nastya/shutterstock

The whole point of bulk-bin shopping, which eliminates packaging costs, is to get a better deal. Look at unit prices and compare them with products on the shelf. While it’s rare, sometimes bulk bin items are more expensive.

## Shop At A Busy Store

![Costco](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/101016_flu_shot_cost_2016_slide_7_fs.original.jpg)Jonathan Weiss/shutterstock

Busy stores have the most turnover, which means bulk-bin items are more likely to be fresh. This is especially important with less-popular items that may not move as quickly.

## Check For Freshness

![woman holding her nose because of a bad smell](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_94wPrM8.jpg)PhotoMediaGroup/shutterstock

Most bulk bins have a strict no-sampling policy, so shoppers must rely on smell and sight to check for signs of spoilage. If you get a whiff of something funky, or see discoloration, it’s best to move on.

## Exchange Spoiled Goods

![woman with groceries waiting in line at the supermarket checkout](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_ImWC4Tx.jpg)Robert Kneschke/shutterstock

Sometimes shoppers get home only to discover that a 10-pound bag of nuts is rancid. Don’t be afraid to bring the goods back to the store with the dated receipt and ask for store credit or an exchange.

## Write Codes On Containers

![thoughtful woman with pen and paper shopping for grocery in supermarket](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_7yIX3MZ.jpg)wavebreakmedia/shutterstock

Bag contents can look similar to a rushed checkout clerk, so be sure to look for item codes and write them down to avoid paying more at the register.

### Trending on Cheapism

- [![A small dog with wet fur is wrapped in a beige towel, being held by a person. The background features blue tiles, suggesting the dog has just had a bath.](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/iStock-2232073702.jpg)**16 Things Americans Keep Paying Someone Else to Do Even Though They Could Easily Do Them**](https://www.cheapism.com/16-money-saving-tips-tasks-you-can-do-yourself/ "16 Things Americans Keep Paying Someone Else to Do Even Though They Could Easily Do Them")
- [![Close-up of Walmart plastic shopping bags filled with groceries on a checkout counter, with a person in the background handling more bags. The bags are labeled “WAL-MART Always Low Prices. Always.”](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GettyImages52802403.jpg)**Walmart Is Becoming the Default Grocery Store for Every Income Bracket. Here’s Why.**](https://www.cheapism.com/walmart-sales-rise/ "Walmart Is Becoming the Default Grocery Store for Every Income Bracket. Here’s Why.")

## Bring A Pen Or Pencil

![metal pen](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_Tkk96Gr.jpg)Pakhnyushchy/shutterstock

Don’t count on the store to provide writing tools to record item codes and other useful information. Those little pencils are easily lost. Bring your own to streamline the experience.

## Leave The Kids At Home

![mother and baby girl playing with toy in living room](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_UnlSrV6.jpg)Oksana Kuzmina/shutterstock

Children can get overly excited in bulk sections — especially those with candy bins. Aside from likely putting their hands in places they don’t belong, they’re likely to beg for unnecessary items and increase the overall cost.

## Try New Things

![assorted olives on farmer's market](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_ByAXH7Y.jpg)MNStudio/shutterstock

They say variety is the spice of life, and bulk bins are full of new smells, textures, and flavors to try. Tasting new things could reveal less-expensive alternatives to your staples.

### Sign up for our newsletter

Subscribe to Cheapism and get exclusive tips, top deals, and money-saving ideas sent directly to you.


Subscribe to newsletter![Loading...](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/themes/oaku/assets/gif/loading-icon.gif)

## Test Before Buying In Bulk

![shop assistant giving customer a sample of meat in a butcher shop](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_9AF64ar.jpg)Kzenon/shutterstock

It’s never a good idea to stock up on something if you don’t know you like it. Upon finding a new product, buy a small amount to sample at home before buying a lot that might go unused.

## Scope Out Storage Space First

![closeup of a woman looking in an empty pantry](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_C8FnGnI.jpg)Steve Cukrov/shutterstock

Before stocking up, map out storage options. How many items will have to be refrigerated or frozen? Are there enough buckets and jars for dry goods? Is there enough space in the pantry?

## Use Stackable Containers

![Rubbermaid Modular Canisters](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_t85GjBD.jpg)Courtesy of amazon.com

Stackable containers are essential for storing efficiently in small spaces. A set of various sizes costs about [$18 on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Rubbermaid-Canisters-Container-BPA-free-1776474/dp/B003BKGJ1A//ref=as_li_ss_tl?ie=UTF8&linkCode=ll1&tag=cheapismsp-20&linkId=2a85a43cad50a136a644206af4dd0740). For bigger storage, opt for pails that nest when empty and stack when full (starting at [$6 with lids from Uline](https://www.uline.com/BL_8172/Square-Pails?keywords=food%20storage)) in square or [round](https://www.uline.com/Product/Detail/S-7914W/Pails/Plastic-Pail-5-Gallon-White) versions.

## Store In Reasonable Portions

![Japanese woman looking into kitchen pantry](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_DAKZy7t.jpg)maroke/shutterstock

Instead of lugging a giant bag out of storage whenever you need just a cup or two of flour or beans, divide bulk items into portions about the size of a normal package. Store these individually wrapped portions together in a large container for neat and easy organization and increased freshness.

## Use Spice Jars

![Rotating Stainless Steel Spice Rack with Glass Jars](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_SGe0t2J.jpg)Courtesy of bedbathandbeyond.com

Likewise, it’s not very convenient to measure a teaspoon of spice out of a large bulk bag, and spices lose their pungency if not they’re used. Keep some low-cost, high-quality spices near with a set of spice jars ( [$23 at Bed, Bath & Beyond](https://www.bedbathandbeyond.com/store/product/rotating-stainless-steel-spice-rack-with-glass-jars/1046981530)).

## Use Scoops At Home

![aluminum transfer scoop](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_w30ou0W.jpg)Stocksnapper/shutterstock

Bulk bins are set up with convenient scoops. Recreate this setup at home to encourage use of the products you buy in large quantities. A set of four scoops is [$9 on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/ChefLand-Aluminum-Multi-Purpose-5-Ounce-Silver/dp/B00QM8DB8W//ref=as_li_ss_tl?ie=UTF8&linkCode=ll1&tag=cheapismsp-20&linkId=308dc66b73c541f0f41db12a152b1c04).

## Use Zipper Bags For Liquids And Freezing

![Ziploc Double Zipper Quart Freezer Bags](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_xBiUHSg.jpg)Courtesy of amazon.com

Zip-top bags are handy for portioning out bulk items to store in the fridge or freezer. They can be rinsed, dried, and reused.

## Use Plastic Bags For Dry Storage

![Great Value Twist Tie Bags](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_MfLYKrk.jpg)Courtesy of walmart.com

Unless a zip-top is absolutely necessary, use simple plastic bags sealed with a twist-tie or rubber band to portion out dry bulk items into smaller, more manageable amounts. They cost less than [$3 for 100 at Walmart](https://www.walmart.com/ip/Great-Value-Twist-Tie-Bags-100-Ct/11303925).

## Use Glass Jars For Safety

![Ball Set of 12 1 Quart (32 oz.) Regular Mouth Canning Jar](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_dZwtjkh.jpg)Courtesy of target.com

Nothing protects food from the elements — including leaching chemicals — better than glass jars with airtight, waterproof seals. Buy them with lids as a one-time investment for less than [$1 each at Target](https://www.target.com/p/ball-set-of-12-1-quart-32-oz-regular-mouth-canning-jar/-/A-12911372), or wash out and reuse jars already in the home.

## Buy A Vacuum Sealer

![FoodSaver V2244 Vacuum Sealing System with Starter Kit](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_r9a7iwA.jpg)Courtesy of amazon.com

Decent vacuum sealers for home use start at less than [$80 on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0044XDA3S//ref=as_li_ss_tl?ie=UTF8&linkCode=ll1&tag=cheapismsp-20&linkId=7da0ac66cafea680bed53c13aab8bdbb) and bag refills cost about 30 cents each. The machine could pay for itself within months.

## Label Everything

![OXO Good Grips 32-Pack Removable Labels](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_M9GJHOG.jpg)Courtesy of bedbathandbeyond.com

Knowing what’s inside containers will reduce the time it takes to find what’s needed and the risk of buying double. Handy labels are [$5 at Bed, Bath & Beyond](https://www.bedbathandbeyond.com/store/product/oxo-good-grips-reg-32-pack-removable-labels/1045879319) for a pack of 32, although a marker and some masking tape also work well. Be sure to include the date.

## Stay Organized

![well stocked pantry](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/101116_how_to_save_money_on_food_slide_5_fs.original.jpg)Darryl Brooks/shutterstock

Keep foods organized in long- and short-term storage containers, storing like with like. For example, different varieties of individually packaged beans can go in one larger bean container, spices in another, and grains in another. This will help you find what you’re looking for and avoid buying something you already have.

## Rotate Goods

![young woman picking a bottle from storage cabinet in kitchen](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/102516_food_storage_guide_slide_35_fs.original.jpg)wavebreakmedia/shutterstock

Keeping things fresh and exciting is key to working through a large stash of bulk items. Rotate base grains, dried goods, and spices to avoid getting sick of the same flavors and textures.

## Snapshot Info On The Bin

![closeup shot of a woman typing on mobile phone](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_kapm1k0.jpg)Rido/shutterstock

Take a quick picture of useful information posted on the bin, such as the exact product name and nutritional details, so you can refer back later when making labels. Look for recipes and rebates, too.

## Use The Freezer

![frozen food in storage containers in the refrigerator](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/010117_unique_ways_to_save_money_on_food_slide_.original_CzQzogs.jpg)BravissimoS/shutterstock

A freezer allows bulk buying of items that would otherwise spoil quickly, such as nuts, seeds, and legumes that contain a lot of fat. Portion them out into small amounts to eat right away and keep the surplus frozen.

## Use The Basement

![spacious empty basement with laundry in house](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_Y2R2RPF.jpg)Artazum/shutterstock

A basement is a natural cellar, with a cool temperature and not a ton of natural light — ideal for food storage. Dedicate a small area of the basement to bulk food and load it with stackable, labeled containers.

## Use The Garage

![clean swept interior suburban garage](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_tengDVY.jpg)trekandshoot/shutterstock

The garage can be handy for storage, but keep items off the floor, even when in airtight containers, and look for a spot that doesn’t get a lot of natural light. A few shelves in the corner can serve as an extra pantry.

## Opt For Nonperishable Foods

![woman in bulk section of grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_85OglNS.jpg)Blend Images/shutterstock

Most bulk bin items are nonperishable, but not all. Watch out: Some dried fruits and candies attract fruit flies and can give off moisture with temperature fluctuations. Stick to foods such as oats, flour, and beans when buying in big quantities to avoid throwing out a portion of your purchase.

## Don’t Forget Nut Butters

![toasted nut butters, pistachio, hazelnut and cashew](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_NtvYCNj.jpg)Nataliya Arzamasova/shutterstock

Ground-to-order nut butters — packed with nutrition and cheaper (by unit price) than prepackaged, chemically stabilized versions — are a popular addition to grocery store bulk sections and typically available to buy in smaller containers.

## Use The Fridge

![woman looking in fridge at kitchen](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_yqrT6IL.jpg)Andrey\_Popov/shutterstock

A few bulk-bin items, such as chocolate, dried fruits, and certain flours, including whole wheat, are somewhere between perishable and nonperishable. Take advantage of the lower price per unit and refrigerate them to extend shelf life.

## Consider A Second Fridge Or Freezer

![home chest freezer](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_BH6RFD1.jpg)ppart/shutterstock

Large families and others who go through a lot of bulk goods may want to invest in a second refrigerator or freezer. It doesn’t need fancy features — just the ability to keep a stable, cool temperature.

## Bring Your Own Bags

![green, sturdy grocery bag](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_tiw8mJK.jpg)Elaine Willcock/shutterstock

A bulk haul demands a few sturdy shopping bags, and as more stores charge for plastic or paper, the costs add up. Bring a few good shopping totes and avoid extra charges.

## Bring Your Own Containers

![pyramid of three food containers](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_QncxEyk.jpg)timquo/shutterstock

Whether stocking up on dried grains, pasta, or even shampoo, avoid the potential cost of using store-provided containers, which can be considerable. Bring your own containers, rinsed for reuse.

## Account For Container Weight

![woman weighing food in bulk section of grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_4DLItNH.jpg)Blend Images/shutterstock

Be sure to calculate the tare weight, or the weight of the empty container, to subtract it from the total and pay only for the product. Writing the tare weight on a container in permanent marker is a good way to remember.

## Double-Bag Flour and Sugar

![flour in a bag on a table](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_BhgHTFW.jpg)Timmary/shutterstock

To prevent spilling at the bins or on the way home from the store, use double bags for potentially messy items such as flour and sugar.

## Be Reasonable

![woman buying cereal in grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/101816_grocery_saving_tips_slide_9_fs.original.jpg)pathdoc/shutterstock

It’s easy to get caught up in great deals and go a little overboard. Stick to reasonable quantities. As a general rule, don’t buy more than your family is likely to consume in four to six months.

## Don’t Mingle Foods In The Store

![close up of female hand pouring nuts to paper bag at grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_jAlysLw.jpg)Syda Productions/shutterstock

A store clerk is liable to ring up a bag of more than one type of bulk food based on the higher-priced item — a few cashews in a bag of peanuts could do it — so keep foods apart.

## Stagger Bulk Buying

![woman shopping for cereal, bulk in a grocery supermarket](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_oRETacA.jpg)Vladyslav Starozhylov/shutterstock

If you shop for most of your staples in bulk, there may not be room in the budget to buy everything at once. Although the price per unit is typically lower, the one-time cost of buying in bulk is higher than the price of a normal size package. Buy some things one month and others the next month to spread out the costs.

## Make It A Group Purchase

![people with shopping carts filled with groceries walking out of Costco store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_1KRlefL.jpg)Kristi Blokhin/shutterstock

If a few people — neighbors, friends, or family — go in on bulk deals and split the goods and the costs, everybody wins.

## Look For Oils and Vinegars

![vegetable oil in plastic bottle on wooden table](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/092916_fall_grocery_list_slide_36_fs.original.jpg)Aleksandrs Samuilovs/shutterstock

It’s becoming more common to find cooking and finishing oils and vinegars in bulk sections. They can be better deals by unit price than packaged versions.

## Avoid Prepared Foods

![trail mix with nuts and fruits](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_tnCaNaD.jpg)Brent Hofacker/shutterstock

Prepared foods consistently cost more than raw materials, and this often applies to bulk foods, too. Instead of stocking up on trail mix, for example, buy the elements separately and mix them at home.

## Stay Away From Sweets

![close up of jelly beans candies and chocolate behind no symbol or circle-backslash prohibition sign](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_MSgrijU.jpg)Syda Productions/shutterstock

Sweets and candy tend to cost a little more than whole, natural foods, and they can be hard to stop eating once you start. Best to avoid them altogether rather than spend more on empty calories.

## Look for Loose-leaf Teas

![black tea in a spoon on a black tea background](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_76bx40J.jpg)Rtstudio/shutterstock

Tea is an affordable everyday indulgence. Make it even more so by buying in bulk, rather than buying a package of individual bags, and use a tea ball at home to make ready-to-drink brewed tea.

## Ask About Specialty Items

![senior salesman assisting female customer in shopping groceries at store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_bohoPEy.jpg)Tyler Olson/shutterstock

Many stores will happily order a new product if requested. If a bulk grocer has run out or doesn’t stock something you want in bulk, ask for it.

## Consider Bath and Cleaning Products, Too

![house cleaning products](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_M0Zi12a.jpg)Sebastian Duda/shutterstock

Non-food items such as dish soap, laundry detergent, shampoo, and body wash are often sold in bulk sections, too, at lower prices per unit and a better deal for consumers.

## Keep Track Of What You Consume

![affectionate woman looking at her boyfriend working on the laptop in the kitchen](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_oFkvLRT.jpg)wavebreakmedia/shutterstock

Jotting down what’s consumed daily or weekly can help clarify how much to buy and when. This can also help families find savings and adjust a budget.

## Buy Small Amounts of Spices

![four spices on wooden spoons](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_XhbDdbs.jpg)Subbotina Anna/shutterstock

If a new recipe calls for a spice you don’t typically keep in the cupboard, head for the bulk bins instead of buying a whole jar. That way the rest doesn’t go to waste if you don’t like the flavor.

## Keep Records of Unit Prices

![woman in supermarket checking shopping list on tablet](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_l5FSniO.jpg)goodluz/shutterstock

Periodically check to see if prices on go-to buys have gone up or down. Keep a record of unit prices to make sure you are not gradually spending more on the same item.

## Ask About Special Promotions

![woman looking at salesman using digital tablet in pet store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_d1r8reX.jpg)Tyler Olson/shutterstock

Many stores offer deals that may not be prominently advertised, including discounts on buying over a certain weight from the bulk section. Have a quick chat with a manager to get the inside scoop.

## Use Coupons

![woman in grocery aisle of supermarket with coupons](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_u1nIDCp.jpg)Monkey Business Images/shutterstock

Bulk foods are usually good deals already, but shoppers can save even more by combining the savings with store coupons offered from time to time.

## Take Advantage of Bulk Foods Week

![large selection of bulk dry foods in grocery store](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/101116_how_to_save_money_on_food_slide_4_fs.original.jpg)James Mattil/shutterstock

One week every October is set aside as Bulk Foods Week. Some 1,600 stores nationwide were expected to take part last year, some with special discounts — making the week a good time to schedule a trip to the bins.

## Know Before You Go

![smiling young woman using laptop in the kitchen at home](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/022117_bulk_food_shopping_and_storage_tips_slid.original_LyjEW2b.jpg)wavebreakmedia/shutterstock

Type in a location or ZIP code at the website [Zero Waste Home](https://zerowastehome.com/) to find stores with bulk bins. The site even includes filters for such things as pasta and pet food.

## Meet the Writer

[![svg%3E](https://www.cheapism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1601104_666228186546_444163080_a.original-570x570.jpg)](https://www.cheapism.com/tess-rose-lampert/ "Tess Rose Lampert")
